text: The paper shows examples of (1) open and closed OSF links; (2a) citation of retracted papers, (2b) citations without a doi, (2c) citations with Pubpeer comments, (2d) citations in the FLoRA replication database, and (2e) missing/mismatched/incorrect citations and references; (3a) R files with code on GitHub that do not load libraries in one location, (3b) load files that are not shared in the repository, (3c) lack comments, and (3d) have absolute file paths; (4) imprecise reporting of non-significant p-values; (5) tests with and without effect sizes; (6) use of "marginally significant" to describe non-significant findings; (7) a power analysis reporting some of the essential attributes; and (8) retrieving information from preregistrations.
rationale: Abstract lists what the demo paper illustrates; the phrase is mentioned in quotes, no result is described as marginal.

text: On average researchers in the experimental (app) condition made fewer mistakes (M = 9.12) than researchers in the control (checklist) condition (M = 10.9), t(97.7) = 2.9, p = 0.005, d =0.59.
rationale: Significant result (p = 0.005) reported plainly.

text: On average researchers in the experimental condition found the app marginally significantly more useful (M = 5.06) than researchers in the control condition found the checklist (M = 4.5), t(97.2) = -1.96, p =0.152.
rationale: Own result with p = 0.152 described as 'marginally significantly more useful'.

text: There was no effect of experience on the reduction in errors when using the tool (p > .05), as the correlation was non-significant (Figure 2).
rationale: Non-significant result described as no effect; imprecise p is another module's concern.

text: We recruited 120 undergraduate students who participated for course credit.
rationale: Filler.

text: The effect of condition on recall did not approach significance, t(118) = 0.41, p = .68.
rationale: Negated: says the result was nowhere near significant.

text: Estimated marginal means were significantly higher in the training group than in the control group, F(1, 118) = 9.20, p = .003.
rationale: 'marginal means' is a statistical term; the result is significant.

text: The linear trend was significant, F(1, 118) = 12.40, p < .001, indicating that response times increased across blocks.
rationale: Trend analysis with a significant result, not a 'trend towards significance'.

text: The interaction was marginally significant, F(1, 118) = 3.10, p = .08, suggesting that training was more effective for novices.
rationale: Own p = .08 called marginally significant and interpreted as an effect.

text: Smith and Jones (2015) reported that the priming effect was only marginally significant in their second study.
rationale: Describes another paper's result, critically.

text: Describing p values between .05 and .10 as marginally significant inflates the Type I error rate, and we therefore avoid this practice.
rationale: Discusses the term; no result is described with it.

text: Previous work found an effect that approached significance (Lee, 2010), but we did not replicate it here, t(88) = 0.20, p = .84.
rationale: The near-significance claim is about Lee (2010); own result reported as non-replication.

text: All analyses were conducted in R.
rationale: Filler.

text: The difference between groups was close to significance, t(88) = 1.80, p = .075, and in the predicted direction, which supports our hypothesis.
rationale: Own p = .075 taken as support for the hypothesis.

text: The effect of age was borderline significant (p = .05).
rationale: p reported as exactly .05; whether it is above alpha depends on rounding and the stated alpha.

text: The correlation between anxiety and performance fell just short of significance, r(58) = -.24, p = .06, indicating that more anxious participants tended to perform worse.
rationale: 'fell just short of significance' and interpreted as an effect; not in the module's term list.

text: There was a hint of an effect of mood on generosity, t(58) = 1.70, p = .09.
rationale: 'a hint of an effect' for p = .09.

text: Participants in the reward condition were faster than those in the control condition, t(58) = 1.85, p = .07, demonstrating that rewards improve performance.
rationale: p = .07 described as demonstrating an effect, without any marginal wording.

text: The main effect of gender was not significant, F(1, 58) = 2.90, p = .09.
rationale: p in (.05, .10) correctly reported as non-significant; guards a future p-range trigger.

text: Response times showed a trend toward significance for the congruency effect, t(58) = 1.90, p = .06, consistent with our prediction.
rationale: 'trend toward significance' for own p = .06.

text: See Table 2 for effects that were marginally significant.
rationale: Whether any result is so described and how it is interpreted depends on Table 2, which is not in the fixture.

text: Although the effect was not significant, it was in the expected direction, t(40) = 1.10, p = .28.
rationale: Reported as not significant; no near-significance language.

text: The three-way interaction was almost statistically significant, F(2, 80) = 2.90, p = .06, and we interpret it as preliminary support for the model.
rationale: Own p = .06 called almost significant and interpreted as support.

text: The manipulation had no effect on arousal, and the test was nowhere close to statistical significance, t(40) = 0.30, p = .77.
rationale: Negated ('nowhere close to').

text: Marginal significance is a contested concept, and Olsson-Collentine et al. (2019) documented how often it is invoked in psychology.
rationale: Discussion of the concept.
